ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure is a table of the first 30 samples of the unit sample response h[n], listing n and h[n] in two columns. The left column can be read as h[0]=1, h[1]=2, h[2]=7, h[3]=20, h[4]=61, h[5]=182, h[6]=547, etc.; the right column continues to give larger values from n=15 to 29. Reasoning: First test the first-order constant-coefficient recursion h[n]=c h[n-1]. From the first few terms in the figure, h[1]/h[0]=2/1=2, h[2]/h[1]=7/2=3.5, h[3]/h[2]=20/7, which are not equal, so the first-order model does not hold. Then fit the second-order recursion h[n]=a h[n-1]+b h[n-2]. Using h[0]=1, h[1]=2, h[2]=7, h[3]=20, there are 7=2a+b, 20=7a+2b. Solving gives a=2, b=3. Check h[4]=2·20+3·7=61, consistent with h[4]=61 in the figure; h[5]=2·61+3·20=182, also consistent with the figure. Therefore the shortest recursion order is 2. The minimum constant-coefficient recursion order of the unit sample response of an LTI system equals the denominator order of the system transfer function, that is, the number of poles, so this system has 2 poles.
